Fifty covers, and the last thing to go down is the water.

The table is built from the centre outwards, because the centre is the only line that has to be straight and everything else is measured off it. Nine candlesticks, none of them lit, because a candle lit before the guests arrive is a candle half gone by the second course.

The room stays like this for about forty minutes. Then it is never this quiet again.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. Brigade, field kitchen and service, carried into rooms that have neither.

The dossier asks the same seven questions of every place. Who allows an outside brigade, where the field kitchen goes, how much power is on site, how the vans get in, how late we can stay, who signs the permit, what it costs.

The answers are the reason we can say yes quickly.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. One event a day. Never two.

This is the part nobody photographs.

The room empties over about twenty minutes and stays exactly as it was left. Then two of us take it apart: everything that came in goes back out the same night, through the same door, and the floor is swept before anybody locks up.

By morning there is no evidence that a kitchen was ever here.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. We stay until the room is empty and put it back the way we found it.

Built for lemons, not for people. Vaulted, north-facing glass, and a floor laid to be dragged over.

The pots go to the far wall in October and the room is empty until March, which is exactly the half of the year we are interested in.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number fourteen.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. We open rooms that are not for hire, for one evening, and put them back as we found them.

Eight hours, and it is still not finished.

A stock reduces by two thirds before it is worth anything, and there is no way to make that happen faster. The only skill involved is not walking away.

It goes in tomorrow's sauce. Nobody will taste it as itself.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. One event a day, cooked by hand, in rooms that are not venues.

The same limonaia, with the glass gone black.

Forty covers under the vault. By day the glass doors are what the room is for; in the evening they are only a mirror, so the light stays low and on the table, or the guests look at their own reflection all night. The terracotta pots stay where they are, against the far wall, unlit.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number fourteen, at night.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. Dinners in Tuscan villas, cloisters and historic houses with no kitchen of their own.

A long table stops being one table at about the ninth guest.

After that it is three or four conversations that ignore each other, and the service has to follow them rather than the room: plates go out by conversation, not by side, or half the table is eating while the other half is still talking.

Nobody notices this being done. That is the whole point of it.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. Long tables in Tuscan villas, cloisters and private houses.

An evening is won or lost at the gate.

What comes through it is everything there is going to be: after that, there is no going back. So the list is checked twice on the pavement and a third time before the doors close, and no crate goes over twenty-five kilos, because one person carries it.

At night the same thing goes back out, and the street is left as it was.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. Everything comes in through one door and goes back out the same night.

A porcino is brushed, not washed.

Under the cap it is a sponge: it takes the water in and does not give it back, then throws it all out at once in the pan, so instead of colouring it boils. It is cleaned dry, brush and knife tip, one at a time.

A crate takes an hour. There is no way to do it in half.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. Private dinners in Tuscan villas and historic houses, cooked on site.

A staircase like this is not a passage. It is the first course.

Whoever climbs it arrives at the hall already prepared, which is why nothing is served on it: you go up empty-handed and come down with the trays, never the other way round. The brigade uses the service stair, which in a palazzo always exists and is behind a door that looks like a cupboard.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number fifteen.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. Private venues that are not venues, in Florence and across Tuscany.

A first course is designed backwards, from the table to the kitchen.

Fifty plates go out in six minutes or they do not go out: which means the pasta goes into the water once the guests are already seated, and everything else, the stock, the sauce, the hot plates, has been ready for an hour. At the last moment you do only what could not be done earlier.

The rest of the evening is decided here, and nobody notices.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. Fifty covers out of a field kitchen, in houses that have none.

The piano nobile is on the first floor, and that is the whole problem.

No service lift, a narrow back stair, and eighty kilos of equipment going up by hand in twenty-five kilo crates. The site visit is for counting the steps and measuring the door at the top, not for looking at the frescoes.

Ninety-one rooms in this dossier. Number sixteen.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. We open rooms that are not for hire, for one evening, and put them back as we found them.

Roughly half the people we cook for are American, Russian or Asian, and we work in English throughout.

The kitchen travels. The base does not.

Syntonia — a travelling kitchen based in Florence. We open rooms that do not open.
